The same mechanism applies for all IPO's and secondary issues and various securities including stocks, bonds and converts.  The goal of the underwriter is to get the corporation the best possible terms, including size and price while also providing a price and size that investors find attractive.  The investor and the company are in direct opposition for the specific transaction but  corporations are also interested in long term goals

Green shoe  101

There seems to be some misunderstanding of the underwriting mechanism in general and the green shoe in particular so let me give it a shot

When a company issues securities a bank or a syndicate of banks handles the placement of the securities to end investors

Of being able to raise cash over many years of deals.  Investors also compete with each other for deals and may have incentive to pay up to get a full sized position on one go.   

Anyway that's not the point of this thread.  What I want to cover is the techniques underwriters use to ensure that the deal once priced and allocated trades well and is stable at around the original issue price or higher

Liquidity very poor leading to thin trading and volatile prices.   So despite the desire to find great long term investors the company and the underwriter want to place some of the deal in more price sensitive investor hands.  Let's call these investors "flippers".  An allocation to flippers is key to a successful deal.

The lead manager of the underwriting syndicate manages that process.  It starts with allocation.  One super tricky problem is if an IPO is issued to long term investors who literally want to put the issue away in their portfolio and never sell that allocation would make post deal

However if an underwriter allocates to entirely flippers the deal will be 100% for sale up a few points the next day and long term investors will be needed to be found after the deal.  Very inefficient.  So there is a mix of investors that are sourced. Some who are known flippers, some who claim long term investment , and some whom are both and will formally or informally place after market orders with the underwriter to buy more or to sell at a price or do both

The third way is for the underwriter syndicate lead by the lead manager to use their own capital to go long the shares in the aftermarket to support the deal and short them in the aftermarket to avoid the deal price from spiking to high.  

Before the deal is placed the syndicate can allocate more shares than the company wants to sell and be short at the deal price

So allocation is the first way to ensure stable prices at or above the issue price and some aftermarket volumes for investors who don't participate in the underwriting. 

As mentioned the underwriter encourages deal participants to place both sell and buy orders in the aftermarket. Thats the second way of delivering stable liquid aftermarket's

This last strategy is risky to overallocate because a rise in price will cost the underwriter syndicate losses 

This is why the green shoe option was invented.  Typically the green shoe allows the underwriting syndicate to purchase 15% more of the share from the company at the original deal price.  So upon allocation the underwriting syndicate allocates 115% of the deal to investors

The green shoe option needs to either be exercised or not relatively rapidly as the underwriting syndicate is restricted from certain market operations until the green shoe is dealt with and the deal breaks syndicate.  Typically this isn't a big deal.  The deal either needs support as it's priced too high or there are too many flippers or the size was too big OR

This means that the syndicate is now short 15% of the deal but is long a call struck at the deal.  If the deal needs support they can buy back the short.  If the deal doesn't need support and trades solidly over the issue price the underwriter exercises the green shoe option to close out their short

It goes fine and the green shoe is exercised.  

Today the green shoe on $ANT was exercised because the lead manager understood the allocation, had orders in their pockets of after market buying from real investors, and perhaps in the aftermarket built up a short position at the

Open or during the trading day above the 15% they were already short. But perhaps more importantly the deal traded all day substantially above the deal price despite horrible broad market action. 

So while it's true that the exercise of the green shoe covered the underwriters 15% short which is ammo to support the deal.  It's also true that the lead manager has all the picture and their own position and capital to assure the deal remains stable for a couple of days.  Once time has elapsed the need to maintain deal stability ends. By Tuesday the issue should trade freely.

PwC signed clean opinions on the accounts and financial reporting controls on 25 February 2026. Its only critical audit matter was “inventory valuation and excess purchase commitments”

No revenue “critical audit matter” doesn’t mean no revenue testing... revenue testing is a pre-requisite as becomes a key area of fraud risk but it depends whether the testing they’ve done is “sufficient”

But with an SEC accounting probe now reported, PwC’s risk assessment and the evidence supporting its “clean” opinion deserve serious scrutiny

I covered this earlier in Jan regarding PCB bottlenecks with photonics + $AMZN Kuiper / $SPCX starlink supply chains.

But as an update, it like other industries outside of AI are really starting to feel the pain now too.  

Global Electronics Association: "Is issuing this Industry Alert on escalating shortages across the printed circuit board (PCB) supply chain. 

Companies in automotive, industrial, medical, defense, and telecommunications report longer lead times and difficulty securing supply as AI absorbs scarce capacity, effectively putting production at risk"

The association meaningful relief unlikely before mid-2028. The association urged buyers to plan ahead for supply constraints and manufacturers.

Hyperscalers like $AMZN already planned ahead of time taking stakes in Gold Circuit Electronics (2368) for supply procurement... 

But can't say the same about other industries procurement (medical industry is probably not used to competing with hyperscalers over the same supply lol). 

The resulting shortages of critical materials, including CCLs and fibreglass cloth, are squeezing supplies for consumer electronics.

TLDR: same bottleneck, same timeline for 2028. It's just interesting to see association warnings about it impacting medical to defense industries. 

So there's incremental information that it's become an industry wide allocation issue. 

I also think it's helpful to see escalating shortages + broadening... so it might show the selloff is starting to look very disconnected with fundamental demand.

tweets.text:
The Fed is turning from a tailwind into a headwind.

Our US Policy LEI leads real yields by about 12 months and has dropped from 66 to 37 in three weeks. 

It is now below 50 for the first time since March 2024 and closing in on the hiking regime threshold of 35.

The last time it fell this fast from a high level was in the spring of 2021. It bounced within weeks before sliding for the rest of the year. 

Real yields followed about a year later and rose from deeply negative to almost 2% through 2022.

Real yields are what money earns after expected inflation, so every other investment ends up measured against them. They are already back at 2.4% and have not been this high since late 2023.

That is the bar growth stocks and crypto now have to clear.

The standing repo facility also mostly just smooths out the issue. The Fed doesn't want persistent facility usage. When it starts to happen it's a sign for them to shift in the coming weeks/months toward gradual balance sheet expansion, like in Q4 2025. That was just like 2019 but more prepared for.

Slightly different than QE since it wasn't about buying duration, but putting out treasury/repo liquidity fires is something the Fed will do whatever the prevailing inflation rate is. It just usually takes less balance sheet expansion than sensationalists would typically predict. A little goes a long way at those times.

THE DAILY METALS PULSE | NOVEMBER 20 — WEEKLY CLOSE

#Uranium #Silver #Gold #Copper

☢️ Spot uranium held near $90/lb this week. By Friday’s U.S. close, the Sprott Uranium Miners ETF ($URNM) had lost roughly 15% in five sessions. During that same week, Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power invited bids for about 13.2 million lb of uranium concentrate for delivery from 2028 through 2037. Bids are due December 28.

🇺🇸 Friday brought the inflation reading I was watching this morning. U.S. households now expect 3.7% inflation over the next year, down a full percentage point from October. Fed Governor Lisa Cook still made the case for higher rates. The Nasdaq fell more than 5% as tech selling intensified after Reuters reported that the SEC was examining Nvidia’s accounting practices.

🥇 Gold was bid near $3,525/oz around 4 p.m. New York time, down roughly 9% from last Friday. 🥈 Silver fell from $48.77 to $40.85 over the same stretch. That’s a 16% loss in a week.

🔶 December copper traded near $5.50/lb on Friday, down from $6.09 a week earlier. Shanghai Futures Exchange stocks rose by 3,204 tonnes to 30,846 tonnes. Even after that increase, those warehouses held less than one day’s worth of Chinese copper consumption.

I remain bullish on uranium. What this week sharpened for me is the financing risk. A developer whose shares fall 15% has to issue nearly 18% more shares to raise the same cash. With utilities already seeking supply through 2037, I’m watching which developers can secure a contract a lender will back and get their mines built in time to deliver.

Follow @Swedish_Uranium for the daily metals pulse.

An update on something I’ve been messing around with given the recent market stress: a cross-asset regime model that asks a pretty simple question — when has the market looked like this before?

The latest reading is interesting. All 10 of the closest historical analogs are now stress / risk-off regimes, with October 2018 the closest match at 78% similarity.

October 2018 is an interesting comparison. Markets were dealing with rising Treasury yields, a more hawkish Fed, trade tensions and a pretty sharp reset in equity valuations — real market stress, but not a financial-system crisis.

That doesn’t mean today is 2018, or that we’re headed for a crisis. But the current mix across equities, rates, credit, volatility, FX and commodities is increasingly starting to resemble periods when markets were under meaningful pressure.

And maybe the most interesting part: what happened next in those historical periods was far from uniformly bearish.

David Friedberg: Restricting Open Source AI is a Path to Tyranny

“Open source needs to be allowed and frankly encouraged to proliferate because the absence of that means that you're going to have tyrannical groups, ultimately, they become tyrannical.

They don't intend to be tyrannical, but every group that has the power to control what people see, what they're allowed to do, what they're allowed to access, how they're allowed to use things, what those specific weights are on ‘facts of history,’ on ‘proven science,’ on ‘the truth.’

That is where people become tyrannical because they have an opinion where they think they're right, and if they have the power, they will act on that opinion, and it will ultimately give them tyrannical force over a broader population.

That's what will happen if we limit the proliferation of open source software in AI.

And I've said it before, I'll say it again, ultimately, you can regulate, you can restrict, you can control, you can litigate, you can criminally penalize people for the outputs of what they use software to do.

But to limit software, to label software, to make it a point of restriction and control creates a regulated monopoly for the closed source products that are out there that ultimately, if aligned with certain government agencies, gives those government agencies and those individual corporations power and control over you, the individual, what you're allowed to do, what you're not allowed to do, and every business on Earth no longer operates freely.

None of us should want that. I don't care what your political affiliation is.”

thread_tweets.text:
Today doesn’t fit a V-shaped reversal because the Fed is max hawkish. A short-term bounce can happen regardless, as it’s mechanical after a capitulation day. Nvidia’s SEC accounting probe, reported late in the session, could be largely priced in unless the findings are very negative. Too soon to tell. It's going to be very noisy. 

I’ll be tracking the SEC probe, and watching for when/if Fed officials say tighter financial conditions are doing part of the work (no sign of that yet despite the crash). A trend change likely needs the Fed to change its tune, unlikely before the Dec/9 FOMC. Or an unexpected Iran deal. 

For 2027 the market hinges on AI revenue/capex and Anthropic is key. It has said growth slowed due to compute constraints, not faltering demand. So it will be crucial to see if its revenue ramps up in line with its new compute or not.

Most people “invest” when they know they can’t handle volatility

But if you invest and panic when markets are down - that is an absurd thing if you think about it

When you consider being wrong you position in a way that doesn’t take you out from being wrong while when right doing extraordinary 

That’s the foundation of investing - asymmetry positioning

I've been playing with Gemini 4 Neon for 5 straight days. Google gave me early access and sponsored today's episode.

10 insights using Gemini 4 Neon (for people who want to make cool things with AI):

1. Type /swarm and give it a researcher, a designer and a couple of engineers. I'd point it at a small directory or app for a niche and let it run overnight. 

2. The physics are so good that I'd mock up a hardware product or a little game with it before spending a dollar on either.

3. I gave it my company's messy invoices and asked for a financial model. Now I go back and forth with it like I've got a CFO on call.

4. Paste in a local business's website and it'll read the whole thing and build them something useful, like a calculator or a new homepage. Interesting cash flow idea there.

5. Make a mini game or a 3D customizer for your product and put an email box in front of it. It's way more fun than a PDF, and people share them.

6. Drop every customer call from last quarter into AI Studio and ask it what you promised and never shipped. It can hold about a million tokens at once, and it stays sharp the whole way through.

7. It's the best model I've tried for the boring stuff like lead routing, CRM cleanup and reconciling invoices. Surprisingly darn good at business workflows.

8. For everyday work, pick Orchestrator in Antigravity. Neon does the thinking and hands the typing to Hydrogen, which is a lot cheaper.

9. Set the thinking to high and build in Antigravity, even though the app still has some catching up to do. The same model scored three times higher there on a coding test.

10. It's a really good writer once you tell it to drop the em dashes. It's also brief, so ask for more when you want more.

TLDR; it's a REALLY good money for WAY cheaper than we're used to. So, you can be way more loose on the types of projects you build and agents you have running.

Link to full ep: http://youtube.com/watch?v=tCY7zMknCJQ

For anyone who’s been keeping up with the streams, you know I put a collar on my Nvidia position on Monday before earnings. 

This was around $155.

I sold the $165 calls for this week and used that premium to buy the $150 puts. The premium covered 77.5% of the cost and I ended up paying a $0.90 debit for the hedge.

I have just exercised those puts and sold my Nvidia position at $150. 

I started buying this name during DeepSeek and ended up getting to an average of $120. Ever since the Jensen news came out, I have felt incredibly uneasy about the position, especially going into earnings given the name couldn’t break out with Jensen on the call so I had no reason to believe it could break out without him.

The risks are simply too high with Nvidia even though the valuation obviously is cheap beyond imagination, assuming the earnings growth continues to be true. The credit backstops, China issues, Jensen not being there…these things could work out but the risk to them at this moment obviously is much higher than normal. The investigation itself is an annoying overhang on the stock regardless of their growth. 

I’ve bagheld various names down and stuck with the story, many times with Nvidia in early 2025, but I was not willing to baghold this name because of Jensen’s affairs. I think the majority of retail are in this name between $120-$140 and now basically have to make a decision if they think things will change or if this company continues forward without Jensen. 

Nvidia can obviously bounce from here, but it’s less about the price action up. It was cheap at $180 and cheap at $150. I wouldn’t care about buying this back at a higher price than I sold, but there would need to be a reason. Just not interested in this until Jensen comes back, if he does.

tweets.text:
The biggest opportunities right now:

1. build for solving loneliness (the more AI floods everything, the more people crave real human connection, IRL and small social) 

2. build for places with no cameras and no recording (being offline and unseen is turning into the new status symbol)

3. build for the crisis of young men. Millions of guys in their 20s feel completely lost with work, dating, and purpose. Whoever builds real brotherhood, mentorship, and an actual path forward wins a massive market (and helps a ton of people). 

4. build for protecting people's brains (feeds are turning everyone's attention to mush, tools that protect your focus and mood are an easy sell)

5. build for the death of "everyone agrees" (you can find a chart or a podcast clip to prove any point now, people are starving for one source they actually trust)

6. build for day 2, not day 0. Anyone can launch an app in a weekend now. But how can you keep it running, fix the mess, and grow it for 3 years.

7. build for throwaway software (not everything needs to be a $20 a month subscription, tiny apps made for one trip, one wedding, or one group chat are coming)

8. build for people whose ego just got bruised by AI. Millions of smart people are  realizing their job was mostly pattern matching. Help them figure out what they're good for next.

9. build for things that take effort on purpose (when everything is instant and free, nothing feels earned, people will pay for slowness and craft)

10. build for people who miss being told they're wrong. AI agrees with everything you say now. Real rooms where smart people actually push back on your ideas are becoming a luxury.

11. build for skin in the game. The internet is full of free takes and bots. Any platform where people have to put real money, real names, or real work behind what they say wins.

12. build for agents that need to spend money (they're getting virtual cards and budgets, someone builds the spend controls, fraud protection, receipts)

13. build for the end of fake email jobs (half of corporate America knows their job is theater, build the exit ramp for people who want to do real work)

14. build for the friend with great recommendations (nobody trusts Yelp reviews etc anymore because it's all bots and SEO, people will pay one obsessive person to just tell them where to eat and what to buy)

15. build for life after the chat box. Typing prompts already feels old. The best AI products won't look like chatbots at all, they'll just sit in the background and proactively handle things.

16. build for markets too small to matter before (500 lobster fishermen was never worth a team, now it's a  real business if you can figure out what to build value to add to these fishermen lives!)

17. build for helpful without being creepy. AI is getting very personal very fast. Whoever figures out how to make it feel warm instead of weird owns consumer tech.

18. build for small private rooms (the public internet feels like an ad and a bot farm, all the good conversations and deals are moving into small invite-only groups)

19. build for someone taking the blame. AI can write the contract or read the scan, but a machine can't look you in the eye when it goes wrong. People still pay for a human on the hook.

20. build for learning that actually keeps up (a four year degree is way too slow for how fast things move now)

21. build for the anti-AI premium (as everything gets generated, human-made and unpolished become status symbols people pay up for)

note: more trends/ideas http://ideabrowser.com (free to sign up)

22. build for the return to the physical (screens fill with slop, people crave the real world, the hands on, the local, the analog)

23. build for the caregiving wave. The population is aging fast, tens of millions are caring for parents, and the whole burden is landing on families with no support.

24. build for finding things you didn't know to search for (algorithms just feed you more of what you clicked yesterday, people miss stumbling onto something totally different)

25. build for the housing and rootlessness problem (people can't afford to settle down, and the whole idea of a stable home base is up for grabs)

26. build for anti marketing (the slickest, most polished websites now look like AI slop or a scam, sometimes a plain text page from 1998 converts better because it feels like a real person built it)

27. build for agents that sit on hold for you (canceling a gym membership, fighting a medical bill, haggling with your internet provider, aint nobody got time for that)

28. build for software you actually own (people are exhausted from renting 30 different subscriptions every month, pay once and run it on your own machine is a massive wedge)

29. build for stuff that only works locally. The internet feels like one giant mall where every city has the exact same coffee shops and trends. Things that refuse to scale are suddenly cool again.

30. build for the 90% automated, 10% human sign-off model (clients don't actually care if AI did the heavy lifting, they just want one real expert to check the work and put their name on it)

31. build for infinite creative testing. Some brands are lighting money on fire on Meta because their ads die in 10 days. Build an automated pipeline that pumps out 100 fresh UGC and static ad variations a week based on what's actually converting in their ad account.

32. build for cold outreach that doesn't look like cold outreach. Mass blasting 50,000 people with "Hope this finds you well" is dead lol. Build an agent that watches for one specific trigger like a new VP hire or a broken checkout page, builds a custom teardown on the fly, and sends it before a human SDR even wakes up.

33. build for programmatic free tools instead of blog posts. Spin up 200 tiny, hyper-specific calculators, little apps and templates for one niche, rank them, and turn the traffic straight into conversions.

34. build for the food and toxin awakening (people are finally waking up to ultra processed food, microplastics, and why everyone feels sick and tired all the time)

35. build for the death of third places (there is almost nowhere left to just hang out without spending $50, which is why run clubs, saunas, and neighborhood clubs are blowing up)

36. build for people who can't retire at 65. Either they can't afford it or they're going to live to 95 and don't want to spend 30 years watching TV. The second act"market is huge.

37. build for the "undo" button for agents. Giving an AI access to your inbox, calendar, or bank account is still terrifying. Whoever makes it safe to let go of the wheel wins.

38. build for the sports betting and day trading hangover (a whole generation of young people are addicted to gambling on their phones and blowing up their bank accounts)

39. build for the death of the attention span. Smart adults can't even sit through a movie without checking their phone or finish a book anymore, and they're starting to hate themselves for it.

40. build for keeping marriages alive. Couples are stretched thin with work, kids, and money, and traditional therapy is $250 an hour with a waitlist. Anything that actually saves relationships is priceless.

41. build for people who don't own anything anymore. You rent your apartment, lease your car, stream your music, and subscribe to your software. Anything that helps regular people actually own an asset again wins.

KEEP BUILDING

Mathematician @__alpoge__  of @AnthropicAI claims that he used Claude to discover a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, arguably the most significant open problem in mathematics.

thread_tweets.text:
Using our AgentX dataset as a rough estimate of the token mix corresponding to $44k in output, we arrive at an estimate of $125k all in.

It's impossible to say what the shape of this workload actually was. Alpöge describes working on this proof over the course of several weeks, so it's possible that the final proof was a small fraction of the total cost. 

On the other hand, in SemiAnalysis’s internal usage, we observe that human-in-the-loop work doesn't burn many tokens compared to asynchronous agentic work, which is what produced the proof. It’s therefore also possible that the two proof artifacts represent most of the total cost. (3/4)

thread_tweets.text:
The proof comprises two artifacts: a “book” that Alpöge has not released because it is “slop,” spanning 250k+ pages, and a Lean proof of 17.4M lines that is the current object of discussion.

We can estimate the number of tokens in the book based on Levent’s previous papers on arXiv, which average 1,946 tokens in the TeX source per page of output PDF using Anthropic’s newest tokenizer. This implies roughly 487M output tokens.

A randomly sampled 1.5% of the Lean averaged 35 tokens per line, which implies roughly 610M output tokens.

At Fable 5.2’s current price of $40/million output tokens, this comes out to $44k. (2/4)

thread_tweets.text:
The only Anthropic math result that discloses a token count was from August, when an Anthropic researcher told Claude, “Take a real stab at the Riemann hypothesis.” (That August result proved that at least 67.2% of nontrivial zeros lie on the critical line; Alpöge’s result today proves that it all of them do.)

Anthropic disclosed that Claude used 31M tokens in that effort, and the proof artifacts that it released totaled to around 3.3M. Thus, the overhead due to thinking and retrying on the way to a significant mathematical result can be estimated at around 89%.

This factor raises our previous cost estimate to $1.17M. 

This is more than the famous $1,000,000 prize that the Clay Mathematics Institute offers for solving the problem! (4/4)
